claim: SQS stores copies of a message on multiple servers. If a server that holds a copy is unavailable when you receive or delete a message, the copy is not deleted there and you might get that message copy again, so applications must be idempotent.
question: Why can a standard SQS queue deliver a message copy again, and what must the application do?

values.display: isn't deleted on the server that is unavailable
you might get that message copy again
Design your applications to be idempotent

qualifiers.condition: a server holding a copy is unavailable at receive or delete time

evidence.quote: If this occurs, the copy of the message isn't deleted on the server that is unavailable, and you might get that message copy again when you receive messages. Design your applications to be idempotent (they should not be affected adversely when processing the same message more than once).

claim: With short polling, SQS samples a subset of its servers and returns messages from only those servers.
question: Which servers does SQS query when a consumer uses short polling?

values.display: samples a subset of its servers
returns messages from only those servers

qualifiers.scope: SQS ReceiveMessage, standard and FIFO queues

evidence.quote: When you consume messages from a queue (FIFO or standard) using short polling, Amazon SQS samples a subset of its servers (based on a weighted random distribution) and returns messages from only those servers.

claim: With short polling, a particular ReceiveMessage request might not return all of your messages.
question: Does a single short-polling ReceiveMessage request always return all messages in the queue?

values.display: might not return all of your messages
a particular ReceiveMessage request

evidence.quote: Thus, a particular ReceiveMessage request might not return all of your messages.

claim: Short polling is the default. The ReceiveMessage request queries a subset of servers and sends an immediate response, even if no messages are found.
question: Which polling type does SQS use by default, and when does it respond?

values.display: Short polling (default)
even if no messages are found

evidence.quote: Short polling (default) – The ReceiveMessage request queries a subset of servers (based on a weighted random distribution) to find available messages and sends an immediate response, even if no messages are found.

claim: With long polling, ReceiveMessage queries all servers and responds once at least one message is available. An empty response is sent only if the polling wait time expires.
question: Which servers does SQS query with long polling, and when does it send an empty response?

values.display: queries all servers for messages
sent only if the polling wait time expires

evidence.quote: Long polling – ReceiveMessage queries all servers for messages, sending a response once at least one message is available, up to the specified maximum. An empty response is sent only if the polling wait time expires.

claim: Long polling helps reduce the cost of using SQS because it reduces the number of empty responses and of false empty responses (messages are available but not included in a response).
question: How does SQS long polling reduce cost?

values.display: reducing the number of empty responses
false empty responses

evidence.quote: Long polling helps reduce the cost of using Amazon SQS by reducing the number of empty responses (when there are no messages available for a ReceiveMessage request) and false empty responses (when messages are available but aren't included in a response).

claim: Long polling is in effect when the wait time of the ReceiveMessage API action is greater than 0.
question: What makes an SQS ReceiveMessage call a long-polling call?

values.display: greater than 0, long polling is in effect
wait time for the ReceiveMessage API action

evidence.quote: When the wait time for the ReceiveMessage API action is greater than 0, long polling is in effect.

claim: To avoid HTTP errors, the HTTP response timeout for ReceiveMessage requests must be longer than the WaitTimeSeconds parameter.
question: How must the HTTP response timeout of a long-polling client relate to WaitTimeSeconds?

values.display: longer than the WaitTimeSeconds parameter
To avoid HTTP errors

evidence.quote: To avoid HTTP errors, make sure that the HTTP response timeout for ReceiveMessage requests is longer than the WaitTimeSeconds parameter.

claim: When the in-flight message limit is reached while a consumer uses short polling, SQS returns an OverLimit error until some in-flight messages are deleted.
question: What happens at the in-flight message limit when the consumer uses short polling?

values.display: will return an OverLimit error
until some in-flight messages are deleted

qualifiers.condition: short polling and in-flight limit reached

evidence.quote: When using short polling – If this limit is reached while using short polling, Amazon SQS will return an OverLimit error, indicating that no additional messages can be received until some in-flight messages are deleted.

claim: When the in-flight message limit is reached while a consumer uses long polling, SQS does not return an error. It returns no new messages until the number of in-flight messages drops below the limit.
question: What happens at the in-flight message limit when the consumer uses long polling?

values.display: does not return an error
will not return any new messages

qualifiers.condition: long polling and in-flight limit reached

evidence.quote: When using long polling – If you are using long polling, Amazon SQS does not return an error when the in-flight message limit is reached. Instead, it will not return any new messages until the number of in-flight messages drops below the limit.

claim: In a delay queue, every message sent to the queue stays invisible to consumers for the delay period.
question: What does an SQS delay queue do to a new message?

values.display: remain invisible to consumers
for the duration of the delay period

evidence.quote: If you create a delay queue, any messages that you send to the queue remain invisible to consumers for the duration of the delay period.

claim: A delay queue hides a message when it is first added to the queue. A visibility timeout hides a message only after a consumer receives it from the queue.
question: What is the difference between an SQS delay queue and a visibility timeout?

values.display: hidden when it is first added to queue
only after it is consumed from the queue

evidence.quote: The difference between the two is that, for delay queues, a message is hidden when it is first added to queue, whereas for visibility timeouts a message is hidden only after it is consumed from the queue.

claim: Changing the per-queue delay setting does not affect messages already in a standard queue. In a FIFO queue the change is retroactive and affects messages already in the queue.
question: Does changing the delay seconds of an SQS queue change the delay of messages already in the queue?

values.display: is not retroactive
setting is retroactive

qualifiers.scope: per-queue delay setting; standard versus FIFO queue

evidence.quote: For standard queues, the per-queue delay setting is not retroactive—changing the setting doesn't affect the delay of messages already in the queue.
For FIFO queues, the per-queue delay setting is retroactive—changing the setting affects the delay of messages already in the queue.

claim: A message timer sets an initial invisibility period for one message when it is added to a queue.

values.display: initial invisibility period for a message
when it's added to a queue

claim: A message timer setting on an individual message overrides any DelaySeconds value of a delay queue.

timers on individual messages

claim: A dead-letter queue must be in the same AWS account and Region as its source queue.

values.display: same AWS account and Region
as the source queue

claim: A redrive allow policy can allow all source queues, allow specific source queues, or deny all source queues. By default, all source queues can use the dead-letter queue.

deny all source queues

claim: In a standard queue, message expiry is always based on the original enqueue timestamp, and moving a message to a dead-letter queue leaves that timestamp unchanged.

the enqueue timestamp is unchanged

qualifiers.scope: SQS standard queue and its dead-letter queue

evidence.quote: For standard queues, the expiration of a message is always based on its original enqueue timestamp. When a message is moved to a dead-letter queue, the enqueue timestamp is unchanged.

claim: Best practice is to always set the retention period of a dead-letter queue longer than the retention period of the original queue.
question: How should the retention period of a dead-letter queue compare with that of the source queue?

values.display: longer than the retention period
retention period of a dead-letter queue

evidence.quote: Thus, it is a best practice to always set the retention period of a dead-letter queue to be longer than the retention period of the original queue.
